extracted.intended_audience: investor_relations and financial PR professionals; academic researchers in finance/communication
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for drafting earnings/financial press releases to maximize pickup-worthiness and influence investor reaction, based on empirical content-analysis linking textual features to abnormal returns and wire pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone calibration
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Loughran-McDonald-style financial-domain dictionaries to audit pre-publication tone; aim for tone that matches the underlying performance narrative without engineering false optimism that exposes the issuer to SEC tone-vs-fact challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audit release tone with financial-specific sentiment dictionaries; match tone to actual performance (avoid overstating positivity). Empirical finding: positive-tone releases predict higher abnormal returns even after controlling for earnings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number density
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases with a higher percentage of numerical content are processed by analysts as more substantive and correlate with higher pickup at financial wires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pack numerical specificity (key figures) into the release, especially the lead. Higher percentage of numbers vs. words increases perceived substance and pickup likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower complexity (e.g., lower Fog Index, fewer syllables per word) makes financial press releases more likely to be picked up by general-business outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simpler wording and shorter words/sentences to increase broader media pickup. Measure readability (Fog Index) and reduce jargon where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline tone–payload alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Headline tone should match earnings reality; mismatched headlines (e.g., positive-tone headline over a miss) trigger corrective or downward correction stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure headline framing accurately reflects the core financial result to avoid negative follow-up coverage and market corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: The first sentence should report the key headline number (revenue, EPS, change vs. consensus) in absolute and percentage terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place critical numeric results immediately in the lead—absolute figures and percent changes—to facilitate quick analyst processing and wire pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference-point disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: State the comparison reference (year-over-year, quarter-over-quarter, vs. consensus, vs. guidance) explicitly so investors can apply the prospect-theory frame without inventing one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about what the reported change is relative to (Y/Y, Q/Q, consensus, guidance) because framing relative to different reference points changes investor evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward-looking language calibration
rubrics_metrics.description: Forward-looking statements should use the issuer's standard safe-harbor language verbatim, not innovate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established safe-harbor wording for projections and forward-looking commentary to manage legal risk and avoid introducing unintended tone shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a length sweet spot for earnings releases (approximately 800–1500 words for mid-cap; approximately 1500–2500 for large-cap); excessively long releases reduce per-section pickup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep releases within genre-typical length ranges to maximize pickup; avoid long, dense releases that dilute numerically salient content and reduce wire/editor attention.
